title: George Ritch buys the Club Harlem for Carter's band
summary: Ritch dug cash from his furniture to buy Connie's Inn, renamed Club Harlem, just to keep Carter's band together.

bands.name: Benny Carter and the Club Harlem Orchestra

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: I might also add something else. And this has to do with George Ritch, whose name I just

mentioned. George Rifich was a man about town, who was -- I don't know exactly what he was into, but he was in to things from which he made a lot of money. I guess they would have called him a 'sportsman' or something, you know?

A sporting gentleman, you know. Well George -- we struck up a very, very fine friendship and I went in to this club with my band, he was a great fan of mine and the bands, and this was Connie's Inn, that had been renamed the Club Harlem.

And it was owned by ... I don't know what to call them ... I certainly can't call them hoodlums, because I don't know that they were, but they were gentlemen whom I would call today members of the organization or something, as they had sort of a rivalry with the Cotton Club, which was ... gee, was that owned by Dutch Schultz, Owney Madden or some people, and I don't know what they were in to. You know?

Yes, they are. Okay. So there was something that happened that this club was going to have to go out of business; these people were being forced out -- maybe because of lack of funds. And this was the Club Harlem, which, as I said, had been Connie's Inn -- and George Rifich learned of this. And he said, 'Well, they can't do this to you, you

know, you've got to have a place for your band." You know? He said, "Well how much money is it going to take to keep the place open?" And I think at that time, if I remember right, it was something like maybe $9,000 -- which in 1933 or 2 or whatever it was, was a pretty good piece of money. Something I certainly had no idea of being able to raise.

So George said, "Well, come over to the house tonight after you get through with the gig." So I went up to the house, and we talked it over, and George said, "Well, I'm gonna buy the place" -- and he started raising cushions, you know, and getting up cash from this chair, upholstered chair and from this sofa, and I never saw so much money just being dug up right in front of me.
Sure. Right there. Sure. He said, "Okay" -- and he got in touch with them, and the next day, he became the owner of the Club Harlem.

Yeah, just like that, and they had a show and a line of girls, and everything, you know? And George was quite a character. He'd come in once in awhile and have a drink, and sit around -- he wouldn't drink anything strong because he didn't drink, but I'd say, "George, what's gonna happen about so and so?" And he'd say, "I don't know -- it's your club!" And I'd say, "What do you mean it's
my club?" You know? He just wanted -- his only purpose for buying the club was to keep my band together, and I shall never forget him for it.
